1I (Number Theory)

Words: 135 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 135
1I OurBigBook.com
A reduced positive definite binary quadratic form f=[a,b,c]=ax2+bxy+cy2 satisfies
∣b∣≤a≤c,
(1)
with b≥0 when ∣b∣=a or a=c. Its discriminant of a binary quadratic form is d=b2−4ac<0. The first displayed inequality already gives ∣b∣≤a, while c≥a gives
∣d∣=4ac−b2≥4a2−a2=3a2.
(2)
Taking the positive square root yields
∣b∣≤a≤∣d∣/3​.​
(3)
Moreover, d=b2−4ac≡b2≡b(mod2), so b≡d(mod2). For fixed negative d, the displayed bounds leave only finitely many possible integers a and b, and then c=(b2−d)/(4a) is uniquely determined. Hence only finitely many reduced forms have discriminant d.
For d=−15, the bound gives a≤5​, so a∈{1,2}. The modular congruence condition makes b odd. If a=1, then b=±1 and c=4; the boundary convention ∣b∣=a⇒b≥0 retains [1,1,4]. If a=2, then b=±1 and c=2; the boundary convention a=c⇒b≥0 retains [2,1,2]. Thus the complete list is
[1,1,4],[2,1,2].​
(4)

2H (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 167 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 167
2H OurBigBook.com
Nash's theorem says that every finite game, including a two-player game with two pure choices each, has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.
For player 1, holding p2​ fixed, the expected value of the payoff is
E1​=−Up1​p2​+2p1​(1−p2​)−2(1−p1​)p2​+(1−p1​)(1−p2​)=1−3p2​+p1​[1−(U−1)p2​].
(5)
It is an affine function of p1​. Therefore player 1 chooses p1​=1 when 1−(U−1)p2​>0, chooses p1​=0 when it is negative, and is indifferent when it vanishes. By symmetry, player 2 has the analogous best response.
If U<2, then 1−(U−1)p>0 for every p∈[0,1], so becoming a Dark Lord with probability one is a strictly dominant strategy. The unique equilibrium is
(p1​,p2​)=(1,1).​
(6)
If U>2, each player is indifferent when the other chooses p=1/(U−1). This gives one interior mixed equilibrium, while the two asymmetric pure equilibria arise because a player facing a certain peasant chooses Lord and a player facing a certain Lord chooses peasant. The three equilibria are
(1,0),(0,1),(U−11​,U−11​).​
(7)
Consequently U0​=2​. At the threshold itself there is a continuum of equilibria with p1​=1 or p2​=1, consistent with the question's strict inequalities.

i

Words: 67 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 67
i OurBigBook.com
A reliable transmission rate R means that length-n codes can carry Mn​ messages with n−1log2​Mn​ tending to at least R while the probability measure of the decoding-error event tends to zero. By the Shannon second coding theorem, the supremum of reliable rates is the binary symmetric channel capacity
C(p)=1−h2​(p),h2​(p)=−plog2​p−(1−p)log2​(1−p).
(8)
For small positive p, the binary entropy function has the asymptotic expansion
h2​(p)=plog2​p1​+ln2p​+O(p2),
(9)
so C(p) starts at one bit per channel use and decreases rapidly from one as errors are introduced.

ii

Words: 19 Articles: 1
3G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 19
ii OurBigBook.com
At p=1/2, the output of the binary symmetric channel is independent of its input. It conveys no mutual information, and therefore
C(1/2)=0.​
(10)

iii

Words: 65 Articles: 1
3G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 65
iii OurBigBook.com
If p>1/2, complementing every received bit converts the channel into a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability 1−p<1/2. This deterministic and invertible output relabelling does not change the channel capacity. Since h2​(p)=h2​(1−p),
C(p)=1−h2​(p)=C(1−p).​
(11)
Thus the capacity rises again from zero as p increases beyond 1/2, reaching one at p=1, where every bit is flipped deterministically and can be recovered by complementation.

A context-free grammar is in Chomsky normal form when every production is of one of the forms
A→BC,A→a,
(12)
where A,B,C are nonterminal symbols and a is a terminal symbol. Under this strict convention there is no epsilon production, so such a grammar cannot generate the empty word. Conversion of an arbitrary grammar therefore gives
L(GChom​)=L(G)∖{ϵ}.​
(13)
If ϵ∈/L(G), the two languages are equal. An alternative extended convention permits the exceptional start production S0​→ϵ; under that convention conversion preserves the whole language.

Solution

Words: 118
b OurBigBook.com
Use the CYK algorithm. For a nonempty input word v=v1​⋯vn​, let Ti,j​ be the set of nonterminals that derive the substring vi​⋯vj​. Initialize
Ti,i​={A:A→vi​ is a production}.
(14)
For increasing substring lengths, compute
Ti,j​=⋃k=ij−1​{A:A→BC, B∈Ti,k​, C∈Tk+1,j​}.
(15)
Accept exactly when the start symbol belongs to T1,n​. The proof is a mathematical induction on substring length: a one-letter derivation uses a terminal production, while every longer parse tree has a root production A→BC whose two subtrees yield two adjacent nonempty substrings. The recurrence considers every possible split point and therefore finds exactly all possible roots. For a fixed grammar the algorithm uses O(n3) time. Under the strict form in part (a), it rejects ϵ immediately.

Introduce nonterminals for the terminals and one for the pair bb:
A→a,B→b,C→c,U→BB.
(16)
Because the original start symbol occurs on a right-hand side, take a fresh start symbol S0​. After eliminating the unit production S→T, one grammar in Chomsky normal form is
S0​SUA​→SU∣AS∣CC,→SU∣AS∣CC,→BB,→a,B→b,C→c.​
(17)
The original grammar generates exactly
{aiccb2j:i,j≥0}.
(18)
The displayed grammar generates the same set: AS adds an a on the left, SU adds one bb pair on the right, and CC terminates the derivation with cc. Since the original grammar does not generate ϵ,
L(G)=L(GChom​).​

With the travelling wave coordinate ξ=x−ct, the reaction–diffusion system becomes
Df′′+cf′+rf(1−f)=0,f(−∞)=1,quadf(+∞)=0.
(26)
At the advancing leading edge the healthy-tissue density is small. Put f(ξ)∼e−λξ with λ>0. The linearization at f=0 gives
Dλ2−cλ+r=0,
(27)
so a nonoscillatory decaying front requires real positive roots,
λ=2Dc±c2−4Dr​​,c≥2Dr​.
(28)
The pulled travelling front selects the Fisher-KPP minimum wave speed, and therefore
cmin​=2Dr​.​
(29)
For the initial wound 0<x<W, two mirror-image fronts enter from its endpoints. The left front moves right from x=0 and the right front moves left from x=W, each with speed approximately cmin​. A sequence of sketches would show the initial rectangular depression becoming two smooth monotone transition layers, the zero-density plateau shrinking, and the two layers meeting near x=W/2 before the profile relaxes to S=1. Their meeting time is
theal​≈cmin​W/2​=4Dr​W​.​
(30)
There is an additional local relaxation time of order 1/r if “close to one” is assigned a fixed numerical tolerance, so the displayed estimate is the dominant healing time when W is large compared with the front width D/r​.

One possible open contour begins at t=0 along a ray with Re(1/t)>0, avoids the essential singularity at the origin, and ends at infinity along a ray with Re(zt)<0. For example, when z>0 is real, it may leave the origin along the positive real axis, bend through the upper half-plane, and approach the negative real axis as ∣t∣→∞. At its initial end, e−1/t→0; at its final end, ezt→0. More generally, the terminal ray may be chosen with
argt=π−argz,

Let M(r) be the enclosed mass. A spherical shell of thickness dr has inward gravitational acceleration GM(r)/r2, so hydrostatic equilibrium requires
drdP​=−r2GM(r)ρ(r)​,drdM​=4πr2ρ(r).​
(45)
With ρ=Ar2P, these equations reduce to
P′=−GAMP,M′=4πAr4P.
(46)
For a regular central value P(0)=Pc​>0, the first equation integrates to
P(r)=Pc​exp(−GA∫0r​M(s)ds).
(47)
The exponential function is strictly positive at every finite r, so the pressure and density cannot reach zero at a finite stellar surface. The equations may describe an atmosphere whose density decreases at large radius, but they admit no nontrivial hydrostatic star of finite radius. Therefore
there is no stable finite-radius stellar solution with this relation.​
(48)

Sk​≡∑j=0p−2​gjk(modp).

Rice theorem says that every nontrivial extensional property of programs computing partial functions is undecidable. Equivalently, a nontrivial index set cannot be a computable set.
Let A be such an index set. Replacing A by its complement if necessary, assume that the nowhere-defined function has no index in A. Since the property is nontrivial, choose an index a∈A. If membership in A were decidable, we could decide the diagonal halting problem as follows. For each x, define
ψx​(y)≃{fa,1​(y),undefined,​after the computation fx,1​(x) halts,if that computation never halts.​

If it halts, then ψx​≃fa,1​ and extensionality gives q(x)∈A. A decider for A would therefore decide whether fx,1​(x) halts, a contradiction. Hence A is undecidable.

a OurBigBook.com
A graph G=(V,E) is bipartite when its set of vertices can be partitioned as
V=A⊔B
(116)
so that every edge has one endpoint in A and the other in B. Equivalently, G has a proper graph colouring with at most two colours.

b

Words: 131 Articles: 1
17G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 131
b OurBigBook.com
Suppose first that G is bipartite. As one traverses any cycle in a graph, its vertices alternate between the two vertex classes. Returning to the initial class therefore requires an even number of edges, so G contains no odd cycle.
Conversely, suppose that G has no odd cycle. Work separately in each connected component of a graph, choose a root r, and put
A={v:d(r,v) is even},B={v:d(r,v) is odd},
(117)
where d is the graph distance. If adjacent vertices u,v were in the same class, then ∣d(r,u)−d(r,v)∣≤1 and parity would force d(r,u)=d(r,v). Choose a breadth-first spanning tree. The two tree paths from r to u and v diverge at some last common vertex; their remaining segments have equal length, and adjoining the edge uv gives an odd cycle. This contradiction shows that every edge joins A to B, proving the odd-cycle characterization of bipartite graphs.

An interior equilibrium point of a dynamical system must satisfy

(302)
If ab=1, the unique candidate is

detDF(x∗​,y∗​)=rx∗​y∗​(1−ab).

In the first region the equilibrium has Poincaré index +1, so index considerations alone do not rule out a periodic orbit. In the second region it is a saddle equilibrium of index −1. Everywhere else there is no interior equilibrium, except at a=b=−1, where the segment x+y=1 consists of equilibria.
Every simple closed curve in the convex set Λ bounds a region contained in Λ. A periodic orbit has index +1, equal to the sum of the indices of the equilibria that it encloses. Thus a region with no equilibrium has total index zero, while the region with the single saddle has total index −1; both contradict the index of a planar periodic orbit. At a=b=−1, a periodic orbit cannot cross the equilibrium segment and must lie in one of its two complementary convex regions, where it encloses no equilibrium, giving the same contradiction. Therefore index considerations exclude periodic orbits except possibly when
a>−1,b>−1,ab<1.​

Bloch theorem states that the energy eigenstates of a Hamiltonian invariant under translations by a Bravais lattice can be chosen as Bloch states
Tr​∣ψk​⟩=e−ik⋅r∣ψk​⟩,ψk​(x)=eik⋅xuk​(x),uk​(x+r)=uk​(x).​
(329)
Indeed, the unitary operators Tr​ commute with one another because Tr​Ts​=Tr+s​=Ts​Tr​, and they commute with H by hypothesis. The simultaneous diagonalization theorem therefore lets us diagonalize all translations within each energy eigenspace. Their eigenvalues form a unitary character χ of the additive lattice:
χ(r+s)=χ(r)χ(s),∣χ(r)∣=1.
(330)
Writing χ(aj​)=e−ik⋅aj​ on a primitive basis gives χ(r)=e−ik⋅r. In position space, with (Tr​ψ)(x)=ψ(x−r), this implies ψk​(x+r)=eik⋅rψk​(x). Hence uk​(x)=e−ik⋅xψk​(x) is lattice-periodic. Adding a reciprocal lattice vector to k leaves the character unchanged, so the crystal momentum lies in a Brillouin zone.
For
a1​=2a​(3​,1),a2​=2a​(3​,−1),
(331)
the equations ai​⋅bj​=2πδij​ give the reciprocal basis
b1​=(3​a2π​,a2π​),b2​=(3​a2π​,−a2π​).​
(332)
The reciprocal lattice is triangular, so the first Brillouin zone is its Wigner-Seitz cell, a regular hexagon. Its six corners are
±32b1​+b2​​,±3b1​+2b2​​,±3b1​−b2​​.
(333)
Reciprocal-lattice translations identify these corners in two classes of three. Representatives are
K=32b1​+b2​​=(3​a2π​,3a2π​),K′=3b1​+2b2​​=(3​a2π​,−3a2π​).​
(334)
For example, (b1​−b2​)/3=K′−b2​, while the other equivalences follow by symmetry and reciprocal translations. This gives the requested sketch: a regular hexagon with the vertical edge from K′ to K at kx​=2π/(3​a) and alternating K,K′ corner classes.
For the tight-binding model, introduce the normalized Bloch sum
∣k⟩=Ns​​1​∑r∈Λ​eik⋅r∣r⟩.
(335)
Each hop by ±aj​ multiplies this state by e∓ik⋅aj​. Thus the two-direction nearest-neighbour tight-binding dispersion is
E(k)​=E0​−2λ{cos(k⋅a1​)+cos(k⋅a2​)}=E0​−4λcos(23​akx​​)cos(2aky​​).​​
(336)
Along the boundary edge from K′ to K, kx​=2π/(3​a) and ∣ky​∣≤2π/(3a), so
E(k)=E0​+4λcos(2aky​​).
(337)
For λ>0, it rises from E0​+2λ at either corner to E0​+4λ at the midpoint; for λ<0 the ordering reverses. Globally the two cosines in the first expression can simultaneously equal 1 or −1, and therefore
Emin​=E0​−4∣λ∣,Emax​=E0​+4∣λ∣,band width=8∣λ∣.​
(338)
Each orbital band contains two one-electron states per lattice site because an electron has two spin states. By band filling, a valency of one leaves this band half-filled and the material conducts, whereas a valency of two fills it. A filled band can be insulating only if it is separated from every empty band by a positive band gap.
The first band's maximum is E0​+4∣λ∣. If the second band's minimum is E0​+Δ, a gap exists precisely when Δ>4∣λ∣. Consequently, among the nontrivial fillings described here,
the material is a band insulator when the valency is 2 and Δ>4∣λ∣.​
(339)
For valency one the first band is partially filled. If Δ≤4∣λ∣, the bands overlap or touch, so even at valency two the overlapping energy bands prevent a band insulator.

The chemical potential is the change in internal energy when one particle is added at fixed entropy and volume:
μ=(∂N∂E​)S,V​.
(340)
Equivalently, μ=(∂F/∂N)T,V​ for the Helmholtz free energy.
Let a microstate s have energy Es​ and particle number Ns​. Maximizing the Gibbs entropy subject to normalization and fixed mean values of E and N is the maximum-entropy derivation of equilibrium ensembles. With Lagrange multipliers α, β, and −βμ, vary
−∑s​ps​logps​−α(∑s​ps​−1)−β∑s​ps​(Es​−μNs​).
(341)
The stationarity equation is −logps​−1−α−β(Es​−μNs​)=0. Normalization therefore gives the grand canonical ensemble
ps​=Ze−β(Es​−μNs​)​,Z=s∑​e−β(Es​−μNs​),β=kB​T1​.​
(342)
Here Z is the grand canonical partition function and kB​ is the Boltzmann constant.
For one fermionic quantum state of energy ε, the Pauli exclusion principle permits occupation numbers only n=0,1. Its two grand-canonical weights are 1 and e−β(ε−μ), so its mean occupation is the Fermi-Dirac distribution
nF​(ε)=1+e−β(ε−μ)e−β(ε−μ)​=eβ(ε−μ)+11​.​
(343)
For a free nonrelativistic particle, ε=ℏ2k2/(2m). In a region of area A, the number of wave-vector states in the annulus from k to k+dk, including the two spin angular momentum states, is
2(2π)2A​2πkdk.
(344)
Since kdk=(m/ℏ2)dε, the two-dimensional free-electron density of states is constant:
g(ε)=πℏ2Am​.​
(345)
We now use units in which kB​=1, as in the question. At zero temperature, the Fermi-Dirac distribution is a step function, and hence
N=g∫0εF​​dε=gεF​.
(346)
At positive temperature the same fixed particle number satisfies the exact relation
N=g∫0∞​e(ε−μ)/T+1dε​=gTlog(1+eμ/T).
(347)
Thus
μ=Tlog(eεF​/T−1)=εF​+Tlog(1−e−εF​/T)=εF​+O(Te−εF​/T).
(348)
This is the low-temperature particle-number cancellation for constant density of states. Therefore, for T≪εF​, the mean number of particles in the energy interval [ε,ε+dε] is
g(ε)nF​(ε)dε≃εF​N​e(ε−εF​)/T+1dε​.​
(349)
Finally, compare the internal energy with its zero-temperature value. The thermally excited particles above εF​ and holes below εF​ have equal leading particle numbers, so their terms proportional to εF​ cancel. With x=∣ε−εF​∣/T,
U(T)−U(0)=2gT2∫0∞​ex+1xdx​=6π2​gT2,
(350)
where the integral follows from the fermion-to-boson thermal integral ratio. Differentiation gives the linear low-temperature heat capacity of a two-dimensional Fermi gas:
CA​=(∂T∂U​)N,A​=3π2​gT=3εF​π2N​T.​
(351)
The requested power law is therefore linear in T, with exponent one.

cωa​≪1.

The displayed 1/r fields also describe the radiation zone, so the observation point must satisfy r≫a and r≫c/ω.
Write tr​=t−r/c. The given vector potential and the time derivative of the electric dipole moment give
A(t,x)≃4πrμ0​​∫J(tr​,x′)d3x′=4πrμ0​​p˙​(tr​).
(353)
When taking the curl, differentiating 1/r produces a near-field term of order r−2, while differentiating the retarded time produces the leading radiation term because ∇tr​=−x/c. Hence
B=∇×A≃−4πrcμ0​​x×p¨​(tr​).​

The assumed electric field E=−cx×B and the transversality x⋅B=0 make the Poynting vector
S=μ0​1​E×B=μ0​c​∣B∣2x.

On a sphere of radius R, the power through surface element R2dΩ is therefore
dΩdP​=R2S⋅x=16π2cμ0​​∣x×p¨​(t−R/c)∣2.​

Choose the polar axis along p¨​ and use the angular distribution of electric dipole radiation, for which ∣x×p¨​∣2=∣p¨​∣2sin2θ. Since ∫sin2θdΩ=8π/3,
P(t)=6πcμ0​​∣p¨​(t−R/c)∣2.​
(357)
For the charged particle in simple harmonic motion,
p(t)=qAsin(ωt)ix​,p¨​(t)=−qAω2sin(ωt)ix​.
(358)
Thus
P(t)=6πcμ0​q2A2ω4​sin2(ω(t−R/c)),⟨P⟩=12πcμ0​q2A2ω4​.​
(359)
Here the angular frequency obeys ω=2π/T, and the average uses ⟨sin2⟩=1/2. The dipole condition is
cAω​≪1.​
(360)
Allow the amplitude to vary slowly as radiation removes energy. The mechanical energy is
E=21​mA2ω2,
(361)
so the radiation damping of a harmonically oscillating charge gives
dtdE​=−⟨P⟩=−6πmcμ0​q2ω2​E.
(362)
This is exponential decay with rate γ=μ0​q2ω2/(6πmc). Its half-life is
t1/2​=μ0​q2ω26πmclog2​.​
(363)
Finally, the largest particle speed is vmax​=Aω. Therefore the dipole condition Aω/c≪1 itself implies vmax​≪c, precisely the nonrelativistic limit required by the mechanical energy formula.

Use the continuity equation to write the axial momentum equation in conservative form:
∂z∂​(rw2)+∂r∂​(ruw)=ν∂r∂​(r∂r∂w​).
(374)
Integrating from the axis to infinity, regularity at r=0 and decay of u,w,wr​ as r→∞ eliminate the boundary terms. Therefore the conserved momentum flux of a laminar round jet satisfies
dzdM​=0.​
(375)
Let W(z) be the centre-line velocity scale and δ(z) the jet width. Conservation gives M∼W2δ2, hence Wδ∼M1/2. The axial inertial and viscous terms scale as
zW2​∼δ2νW​,
(376)
so Wδ2∼νz. Combining the two relations gives
δ(z)∼M1/2νz​,W(z)∼νzM​.​
(377)
Thus the width grows linearly and the centre-line speed decays as z−1. The volume flux scales as
Q(z)=∫0∞​rwdr∼Wδ2∼νz,
(378)
so it increases downstream. By fluid entrainment, the extra flux must be ambient fluid drawn radially into the jet.

Let L=[1,−2,1] be the symmetric Dirichlet second-difference matrix on the M interior points. The method is
(aI−4μ−c​L)un+1=(aI+4μ+c​L)un.
(399)
The orthogonal sine vectors diagonalize L, with eigenvalues
ℓj​=−4sj​,sj​=sin2(2(M+1)jπ​),j=1,…,M.
(400)
Because the two time-level matrices are real symmetric polynomials in the same symmetric matrix, they share this orthonormal eigenbasis. Whenever the left matrix is invertible, the amplification matrix is therefore normal, so its Euclidean operator norm is the largest modulus of its eigenvalues. The jth amplification factor is
Gj​=a+(μ−c)sj​a−(μ+c)sj​​.
(401)
For the physical Courant number μ>0,
∣a+(μ−c)s∣2−∣a−(μ+c)s∣2=4μs(a−cs).
(402)
Hence ∣Gj​∣≤1 exactly when a−csj​≥0. Requiring this uniformly for every mesh, whose values sj​ become dense in (0,1), gives
a−cs≥0(0≤s≤1).
(403)
Equivalently, a≥0 and c≤a. Under these inequalities the denominator is nonzero for every 0<s<1: if c≤μ this is immediate, while if c>μ then a≥c gives a+(μ−c)s≥a+μ−c≥μ>0. Thus the necessary and sufficient mesh-uniform stability conditions are
μ>0,a≥0,c≤a.​
(404)
This is the stability of a two-parameter implicit-explicit diffusion scheme. If consistency with the stated diffusion equation is also required, comparison of the leading Taylor terms gives akut​=(k/2)uxx​+o(k), so a=1/2 and the stable consistent family has c≤1/2.
